name: Sydney Opera House
clues: White concrete shells, all cut from one imaginary sphere, sit on a harbour point. Its architect resigned mid-build and never came back to see it finished.
Its architect's competition entry was barely more than sketches, yet it became the most famous performing arts centre on Earth, its sails gleaming on a harbour point near a giant arch bridge.
blurb: The sails are covered in more than a million Swedish-made tiles that clean themselves when it rains. Utzon's winning entry in the 1957 competition was little more than a set of sketches, and working out how to build the shells took years: the answer was to cut them all from the surface of one imaginary sphere. As costs and delays mounted, Utzon resigned in 1966 and left Australia, never to return. A local team finished the building, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1973. Today it hosts more than 1,800 performances a year.

name: Eiffel Tower
clues: Built as a temporary gateway to a world's fair, this wrought-iron lattice was the tallest structure on Earth for 41 years.
blurb: Gustave Eiffel's company built it for the 1889 World's Fair, with a permit for just 20 years. Leading Parisian artists signed a protest against this 'useless and monstrous' tower before it went up. At 300 m (330 m today, with its antennas) it was the tallest structure in the world until New York's Chrysler Building passed it in 1930. Around 2.5 million rivets hold its wrought iron together, and it is repainted by hand roughly every seven years. On hot days the metal expands and the tower grows by up to about 15 cm.

name: Burj Khalifa
clues: Its Y-shaped plan is borrowed from a desert flower, and it has held the world height record since the day it opened.
blurb: At 828 m it's so tall that you can watch the sun set from the ground, ride the lift up and watch it set again. Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it has been the world's tallest building since it opened in 2010. Its Y-shaped floor plan, inspired by a desert flower, steps back as it climbs, which breaks up the wind. The spire alone, about 240 m, is taller than many skyscrapers. Some of its structural steel was salvaged from the demolished Palace of the Republic in East Berlin.

name: Colosseum
clues: Four storeys of arches held around 50,000 spectators; sailors worked the canvas awning that shaded them.
blurb: Begun under Emperor Vespasian in AD 72 and finished under his son Titus in 80, it is the largest amphitheatre ever built. Crowds of some 50,000 to 80,000 came for gladiator fights, animal hunts, executions and re-enacted battles. Under the arena floor ran a maze of tunnels and lifts that hoisted animals and scenery up through trapdoors, and a huge awning worked by sailors could shade the seats. After Rome fell it served as a quarry, a fortress, workshops and even housing, which is why so much of it is missing.

name: Taj Mahal
clues: A white marble tomb for a beloved wife at the end of a quartered garden on a river bank. Its four minarets lean slightly outwards, away from the dome.
blurb: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child; he was later buried beside her. Some 20,000 workers are said to have spent over two decades on the complex. The white marble is inlaid with semi-precious stones, while the mosque and guest house on either side are of red sandstone. Everything is mirrored around one axis except Shah Jahan's own tomb, added later. The marble seems to change colour through the day, from pinkish at dawn to milky white at noon.

name: Empire State Building
clues: An Art Deco tower thrown up in just over a year during the Depression. Its mast was meant to moor airships.
blurb: Designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon, it went up in just over a year, at times rising about four and a half storeys a week. It opened in 1931 as the world's tallest building and kept the title for nearly 40 years, until the World Trade Center's North Tower passed it in 1970. Its mast was first meant as a mooring post for airships, an idea quickly dropped as too dangerous. The building has its own ZIP code, and lightning strikes it about 20 times a year.

name: Sagrada Família
clues: A basilica under construction since 1882. Its architect, knocked down by a tram, is buried in the crypt.
blurb: Construction began in 1882, and Antoni Gaudí took over a year later, devoting the rest of his life to it. When he died in 1926 less than a quarter was finished, and he is buried in its crypt. Asked why it was taking so long, he reportedly replied that his client was not in a hurry. Paid for only by donations, it has risen slowly ever since; in 1936 anarchists set fire to the crypt and destroyed many of his plans. Inside, the columns branch like trees into a stone forest, lit by coloured glass. It is now the tallest church in the world.

name: St Basil's Cathedral
clues: Nine chapels under swirling, candy-painted onion domes, at the end of the most famous square in a northern capital.
blurb: Ivan the Terrible ordered it in 1555 to celebrate the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan. It is really several churches in one: eight chapels around a central one, each with its own dome, and a tenth chapel was added in 1588 over the grave of the holy fool Vasily, who gave the cathedral its popular name. Legend says Ivan blinded the architects so they could never build anything as beautiful again, which is almost certainly untrue. The famous bright colours came later; it was completed with them in 1683.

name: Petronas Towers
clues: Twin towers on an eight-pointed Islamic star plan, joined by a two-storey skybridge at the 41st and 42nd floors.
blurb: From 1998 to 2004 these 88-storey towers were the tallest buildings in the world, and they are still the tallest twin towers. Architect César Pelli based their floor plan on an eight-pointed Islamic star. A two-storey skybridge links them at the 41st and 42nd floors. It isn't fixed rigidly to the towers, so it can slide as they sway in the wind. The towers were built by two rival teams, one led by a Japanese firm and one by a Korean firm, which turned construction into a race.

name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
clues: A cathedral bell tower started on soft clay. Wars stopped work for nearly a century, which let the ground settle and probably saved it from falling over.
blurb: It is the bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, and it began to lean during construction in the 12th century because the soft ground couldn't carry its weight. Work stopped for almost a century, partly because of wars, which gave the soil time to settle and probably saved it from collapse. The builders then made the upper floors slightly taller on one side to compensate, so the tower is actually a little curved. By 1990 it leaned 5.5 degrees; engineers spent the next decade removing soil from under the high side, bringing it back to just under 4.

name: Parthenon
clues: A marble Doric temple with almost no straight lines: the columns swell and the floor bows upwards to correct the eye.
blurb: Built between 447 and 438 BC, the temple was dedicated to Athena and also served as Athens' treasury. Its columns lean slightly inwards and its floor rises gently in the middle, subtle corrections that make it look perfectly straight from a distance. Over the centuries it became a church and then a mosque. It stood largely intact until 1687, when a Venetian shell hit gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside. Many of its surviving sculptures were taken to Britain by Lord Elgin in the early 1800s and are still in the British Museum.

name: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben)
clues: A Gothic Revival clock tower on a riverside parliament. The name everyone uses really belongs to the 13-tonne bell inside.
blurb: Big Ben is strictly the name of the great bell, but everyone uses it for the tower too, officially the Elizabeth Tower since 2012. Designed by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin and finished in 1859, it rises 96 m, with 334 steps up to the belfry. The first great bell cracked during testing, and its replacement cracked soon after it was hung, so it still rings slightly out of tune. The clock is famously reliable: old pennies placed on the pendulum fine-tune it, each one changing its speed by about two-fifths of a second a day.

name: Forbidden City
clues: Nearly a thousand red-and-gold buildings behind a moat. For five centuries, ordinary people could not enter without the emperor's permission.
blurb: Built between 1406 and 1420, it was home to 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties for almost 500 years, and ordinary people were not allowed in. Legend says it has 9,999 rooms, one short of the 10,000 of heaven; a survey counted 8,886. Its yellow roof tiles were a colour reserved for the emperor. The last emperor, Puyi, left in 1924, and since 1925 it has been the Palace Museum. It is the largest surviving palace complex in the world, and now one of the most visited places on Earth.

name: Notre-Dame de Paris
clues: A Gothic cathedral on a river island, with flying buttresses and rose windows. Its 19th-century spire fell in a 2019 fire and was rebuilt exactly.
blurb: Building began in 1163 and was largely finished by 1260. Its flying buttresses, rib vaults and huge rose windows made it one of the great works of French Gothic. During the French Revolution much of its religious imagery was smashed. Victor Hugo's 1831 novel about its hunchbacked bell-ringer made it famous again and helped save it from ruin, leading to a major restoration in the 1800s that added the spire. That spire collapsed in the fire of April 2019, and after five years of rebuilding the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

name: Pantheon
clues: A 2,000-year-old temple behind a porch of granite columns. The open eye at the top of its concrete dome lets the rain fall straight onto the floor.
blurb: The building you see was completed by Emperor Hadrian around AD 126, but the inscription on the front still names Agrippa, who built an earlier temple on the site. Almost 2,000 years later its dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The concrete gets lighter towards the top, with volcanic pumice mixed in, and the coffers in the ceiling cut the weight further. It has been a church since 609. When it rains, water falls through the open eye at the top, about 8 m across, and drains away through small holes in the floor.

name: CN Tower
clues: A concrete telecom tower on a lakeshore, with a glass floor 342 m up. It was the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years.
blurb: Built by the railway company Canadian National, hence the name, it was finished in 1976 to send TV and radio signals over Toronto's growing skyline. At 553 m it was the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years, until the Burj Khalifa passed it. It has a glass floor 342 m up and a revolving restaurant at about 350 m. Thrill-seekers can walk around the outside of the main pod on the EdgeWalk, strapped to a rail 356 m above the ground. It is struck by lightning dozens of times a year.

name: Hagia Sophia
architect: Isidore of Miletus & Anthemius of Tralles
clues: A dome that seems to float on a ring of 40 windows. It has been a church, a mosque, a museum and a mosque again.
blurb: Emperor Justinian had it built in just five years, finishing in 537, after riots had destroyed the church before it. For nearly a thousand years it was the largest cathedral in the world, and its huge dome resting on pendentives changed the history of architecture. The first dome collapsed after an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt taller. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453 it became a mosque and gained its minarets. It was a museum from 1935 and became a mosque again in 2020; its Byzantine mosaics are still there, some covered during prayers.

name: Marina Bay Sands
clues: Three 55-storey hotel towers carry a 340-metre 'park' across their roofs, with an infinity pool at the edge.
blurb: Designed by Moshe Safdie and opened in 2010, the resort cost about S$8 billion, then the most expensive casino property in the world. Its three 55-storey hotel towers are topped by the SkyPark, a 340 m platform that looks like a ship balanced on the roofs. The rooftop pool is about 150 m long and sits some 200 m above the bay. The deck overhangs the north tower by about 67 m, the largest public cantilevered platform in the world. Down by the water there is even a floating Apple store.

name: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
clues: Titanium-clad curves on an old industrial riverfront in the rainy north of the Iberian peninsula. Its success turned the host city's name into a byword for regeneration.
blurb: When Frank Gehry's museum opened in 1997, it turned a declining industrial port into a destination, a boost now known as the 'Bilbao effect'. Its curves were designed with CATIA, software made for designing fighter jets. The titanium skin, less than half a millimetre thick, ripples like fish scales and changes colour with the weather. Outside, Jeff Koons's giant Puppy, covered in flowers, guards the entrance, and Louise Bourgeois's huge spider sculpture stands by the river.

name: Neuschwanstein Castle
clues: A fairy-tale castle in the Alpine foothills for a reclusive king, secretly built on a steel frame with central heating. He lived there for only 172 days.
blurb: King Ludwig II of Bavaria began it in 1869 as a private retreat, inspired by medieval legends and the operas of his hero Richard Wagner. Behind the fairy-tale towers it had modern comforts such as central heating, running water and telephone lines. He paid for it from his own fortune, not the state's, but ran up huge debts. Ludwig lived there only a few months before he was deposed and died mysteriously in 1886. It opened to paying visitors weeks later, and it inspired Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.

name: Fallingwater
clues: A weekend house whose concrete terraces cantilever straight out over a waterfall in the Appalachian woods.
blurb: Frank Lloyd Wright designed it in the mid-1930s as a weekend house for the Pittsburgh department store owner Edgar Kaufmann and his wife Liliane. The family expected a house with a view of their favourite waterfall; Wright put them right on top of it, so you hear the water throughout the house. Its concrete terraces reach out over the stream, anchored to the rock. They began to sag almost at once and kept sagging for decades, until engineers reinforced them with steel cables in 2002. It has been open to visitors since 1964.

name: Villa Savoye
clues: A white box on thin columns in a town on the Seine, just outside a capital, built as a manifesto of five points. A car's turning circle shaped the ground floor.
blurb: Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret built this weekend house for the Savoye family between 1928 and 1931. It shows his 'five points' of modern architecture: pillars that lift it off the ground, a roof garden, a free plan, long strip windows and a free facade. A ramp leads you up through the house, and the curve of the ground floor followed the turning circle of a car. The roof leaked so badly that the family complained for years, and the house was later nearly demolished. Today it is a protected monument and one of the most influential houses of the 20th century.

name: Chrysler Building
clues: A steel sunburst crown on the most famous island skyline in the Americas. Its spire was assembled in secret inside the top floors and hoisted out in 90 minutes to steal a height record.
blurb: Walter Chrysler paid for it himself as an investment for his children; it was never his company's headquarters. It was racing 40 Wall Street to be the world's tallest building, so the builders secretly assembled its 38 m spire inside the crown and raised it into place in about 90 minutes. It held the title for less than a year before the Empire State Building passed it. Its gargoyles are steel eagle heads and radiator caps modelled on Chrysler cars, and its crown is clad in gleaming stainless steel.

name: Lotus Temple
clues: A Bahá'í house of worship made of 27 free-standing marble 'petals', open to people of every faith.
blurb: Designed by the Iranian-born architect Fariborz Sahba and dedicated in 1986, it is a Bahá'í House of Worship, open to people of every faith. Its 27 marble-clad concrete petals stand in three rings of nine, like a half-open lotus. There is no altar, no clergy and no sermons, yet it draws several million visitors a year. Nine pools surround the building, completing the lotus and helping keep the hall cool. On its completion it was compared with the Sydney Opera House, and it has won awards from engineering bodies around the world.

name: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque
clues: More than 80 white marble domes and reflecting pools on the Persian Gulf coast, with one of the largest hand-knotted carpets in the world inside.
blurb: Built between 1994 and 2007, it is the largest mosque in the United Arab Emirates and was the idea of the country's founding president, Sheikh Zayed, who is buried in its courtyard. It blends styles from across the Islamic world, with 82 white domes and four minarets. The carpet in the main prayer hall, hand-knotted by about 1,200 artisans, is one of the largest in the world, and the main chandelier is one of the largest too. Reflecting pools line the arcades, whose white marble columns are inlaid with flowers in semi-precious stones.

name: Atomium
clues: Nine steel spheres arranged as an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times, built for a world's fair in the capital of a small, multilingual European country.
blurb: Built as the centrepiece of the 1958 World's Fair in Brussels, it shows the unit cell of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times. It was meant to stand for just six months and never came down. Its nine steel spheres, each 18 m across, are linked by tubes holding stairs, escalators and what was then the fastest lift in Europe. Six spheres can be visited, and the top one holds a restaurant with a view over all of Brussels. A renovation in 2004 to 2006 replaced its original aluminium skin with stainless steel.

name: Alhambra
clues: The red hilltop palace-fortress of the last Muslim kingdom in Western Europe, with honeycomb stucco ceilings and a fountain carried by twelve lions.
Arabic poetry is carved into the walls of this palace-fortress, where a queen and king later backed an explorer's voyage west, on a hill facing snowy peaks in southern Iberia.
blurb: Its name means 'the red one', after the colour of its walls. Begun in 1238 on a hill above Granada, it was the palace and fortress of the Nasrid rulers, the last Muslim dynasty in Spain, and most of its famous halls date from the 14th century. Inside, walls and ceilings are covered in carved stucco, tiles and Arabic poetry, and water runs through courtyards such as the Court of the Lions. After 1492 it became a royal court of Ferdinand and Isabella, where Columbus won backing for his voyage.

name: Potala Palace
clues: Thirteen storeys of white and red walls climbing a hill at 3,700 m: for three centuries the winter palace of a line of spiritual leaders.
blurb: From 1649 until 1959 it was the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas. The 5th Dalai Lama began the present building in 1645 on a hill in the middle of the Lhasa valley, about 3,700 m above sea level, so many visitors are out of breath before they reach the top. It rises 13 storeys and holds more than 1,000 rooms. Its sloping stone walls are up to 5 m thick at the base, and copper was poured into the foundations to protect it from earthquakes. The White Palace held living quarters and offices; the Red Palace is devoted to prayer and holds the tombs of past Dalai Lamas.

name: Angkor Wat
clues: The largest religious monument on Earth, rising from the Southeast Asian jungle. It faces west, and its five lotus-bud towers are mirrored in a vast moat.
blurb: The Khmer king Suryavarman II built it in the early 12th century as a Hindu temple to Vishnu; it later became Buddhist and still is today. It is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five lotus-bud towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and the wide moat for the oceans around it. Unlike most temples at Angkor, it faces west. Its sandstone blocks came from quarries tens of kilometres away, probably by canal. Its galleries carry hundreds of metres of carved reliefs, and it is the centrepiece of Cambodia's national flag.

name: CCTV Headquarters
clues: Two leaning towers joined at the top and bottom into one loop for a state broadcaster in an East Asian capital. Locals call it 'big pants'.
blurb: Designed by Rem Koolhaas and Ole Scheeren of OMA, it is the headquarters of China's state broadcaster. Rather than reaching straight up, its two leaning towers join at the top and bottom to form a skewed loop. The overhanging corner juts out about 75 m in mid-air, and the two halves were joined early one morning, when the steel on both sides was at the same temperature. The irregular grid on its facade is densest where the structure works hardest. Locals nicknamed it 'big pants'.

name: Oslo Opera House
clues: Its white stone roof slopes down into a fjord, so anyone can walk straight up onto it.
blurb: Designed by the Norwegian firm Snøhetta and opened in 2008, it is home to the national opera and ballet. Its white roof slopes down into the fjord, so you can walk straight up onto it, and locals picnic, sunbathe and skateboard there. The angled surfaces are clad in white granite and Carrara marble from Italy, so the building seems to rise out of the water. The main auditorium, lined with oak, seats about 1,360. It is the largest cultural building in Norway since Nidaros Cathedral was finished around 1300.

name: Elbphilharmonie
clues: A glass crown shaped like waves, on top of a brick cocoa warehouse in a big North Sea river port. The main hall is lined with 10,000 unique acoustic panels.
blurb: Designed by Herzog & de Meuron, Hamburg's concert hall sits on top of an old brick warehouse from 1963, its glass crown shaped like a wave or a sail. A curved escalator 82 m long carries you up through the warehouse to a public plaza with views over the harbour. The main hall is lined with about 10,000 gypsum panels, each with its own pattern of dimples to spread the sound. Costs grew to about ten times the original budget and it opened years late, in 2017, but Hamburg got a world-class concert hall.

name: Cathedral of Brasília
clues: Sixteen curved concrete columns reach up like hands, in a capital city drawn from scratch in the 1950s.
blurb: Oscar Niemeyer designed it for Brazil's brand-new capital, and it was dedicated in 1970. Sixteen curved concrete columns, each weighing about 90 tonnes, rise like hands reaching to the sky and hold up a crown of glass. Most of the church sits below ground: you enter through a dark passage and emerge into a bright hall full of coloured light. Angels hang from the ceiling on steel cables, and four bronze evangelists guard the entrance.

name: Taipei 101
clues: Stacked like bamboo in eight-floor segments, with a 660-tonne golden steel ball hanging inside to calm typhoon sway.
blurb: With 101 floors above ground, it was the world's tallest building from 2004 until the Burj Khalifa in 2009. Its design echoes a stalk of bamboo, rising in eight sections of eight floors, eight being a lucky number in Chinese culture. Near the top hangs a 660-tonne steel ball that sways to steady the tower in typhoons and earthquakes; it is so popular that it has its own cartoon mascots, the 'Damper Babies'. Its lifts were once the fastest in the world, climbing from the 5th to the 89th floor in 37 seconds.

name: Habitat 67
clues: 354 prefabricated concrete boxes stacked like a hillside village for a world expo — a student's thesis made real.
Built for a world's fair by an architect still in his twenties: a jumble of identical concrete boxes on a riverside pier in a French-speaking North American city.
blurb: Moshe Safdie developed it from his university thesis and built it in his twenties for the Expo 67 world's fair in Montreal. It is made of 354 identical concrete boxes, cast on site and stacked by crane into a hilly village of apartments. Safdie wanted to give city dwellers a garden, so each unit's terrace is the roof of the one below. It was meant as a prototype for affordable housing, but its flats became sought after instead. Safdie still keeps an apartment there.

name: Kunsthaus Graz
clues: A blue acrylic blob with nozzle-shaped skylights, nicknamed 'the friendly alien', moored beside a red-roofed old town on the eastern edge of the Alps.
blurb: Designed by Peter Cook and Colin Fournier, it opened in 2003, when Graz was European Capital of Culture, and shows contemporary art. The blue acrylic blob, with nozzle-shaped skylights pointing north, sits among the red roofs of the old town like a creature that has just landed. Locals call it 'the friendly alien', and the nickname stuck so well that the museum uses it too. At night its skin becomes a giant low-resolution screen made of 930 fluorescent rings, showing images and messages across the river.

name: Heydar Aliyev Center
clues: A white surface that rises out of the plaza and folds over a cultural centre with almost no straight lines, near an inland sea.
blurb: Zaha Hadid's cultural centre in Baku opened in 2012 and holds a museum, a concert hall and galleries. There are almost no straight lines anywhere: the building rises from the landscape in one continuous white wave. Its skin is made of thousands of panels, nearly every one a different shape. Inside, floors flow into walls and ceilings without a break. In 2014 it won the Design of the Year award from London's Design Museum.

name: National Parliament House (Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban)
clues: Massive concrete walls pierced by giant circles and triangles, rising from an artificial lake in a South Asian delta capital. Its architect died years before it was finished.
blurb: Louis Kahn designed it in the 1960s for what was then East Pakistan, and building work stopped during Bangladesh's 1971 war of independence. It was finished in 1982, eight years after Kahn's death, as the parliament of the new country. The complex covers more than 200 acres, one of the largest legislative complexes in the world. Huge circles, triangles and rectangles cut into its concrete walls let light in while shading the rooms from the sun. Surrounded by an artificial lake, the parliament seems to float.

name: Great Mosque of Djenné
clues: The largest mud-brick building in the world. Every year the whole town turns out in a festival to replaster it.
blurb: It is the largest mud-brick building in the world. A mosque has stood here since around the 13th century, but the current one dates from 1907. Every year the rains wear away its walls, so the whole town joins a festival to replaster it with fresh mud. The palm-wood sticks poking out of the walls are built-in scaffolding for the job, and they also help the walls cope with changes in temperature. Its great facade faces the market square, and the old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Hallgrímskirkja
clues: A concrete church whose stepped front imitates basalt columns formed by cooling lava, towering over a small capital.
blurb: Named after the 17th-century poet and pastor Hallgrímur Pétursson, it is the largest church in Iceland. Architect Guðjón Samúelsson designed it in 1937, and it took 41 years to build, finally finishing in 1986. Its stepped concrete wings are said to recall the basalt columns that form when lava cools. At about 75 m it is one of the tallest structures in Iceland, and a lift takes you up the tower for a view over Reykjavík. A statue of the explorer Leif Erikson, a gift from the USA, stands outside.

name: Niterói Contemporary Art Museum
clues: A flying saucer on a cliff, reached by a red serpentine ramp, looking across a bay at a much more famous city.
blurb: Oscar Niemeyer designed this contemporary art museum, finished in 1996, on a cliff across the bay from Rio de Janeiro. A single central column holds up the whole saucer, which is often compared to a UFO, and Niemeyer described it rising from its reflecting pool like a flower. A curving red ramp leads visitors up to the entrance. Inside, a ring of windows around the gallery frames Guanabara Bay, Rio and Sugarloaf Mountain.

name: Church of St George (Bete Giyorgis)
architect: Commissioned by King Gebre Mesqel Lalibela
clues: Carved downwards out of solid volcanic rock in the shape of a cross, high in the mountains of the Horn of Africa. It stands in its own pit, about 12 metres deep.
blurb: It is one of eleven churches cut straight down into the rock at Lalibela, named after King Lalibela, who commissioned them around 1200. Seen from above, it is a cross carved from a single block of volcanic rock, standing in a pit about 12 m deep. Nothing was built up: everything, from the roof to the windows, was carved down and hollowed out. Legend says angels helped with the work by night. It is still a working church and a place of pilgrimage for Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

name: Jewish Museum Berlin
clues: A zinc-clad zigzag slashed with window cuts, in a capital once split by a wall. Inside are empty 'voids' you can see into but never enter.
blurb: Daniel Libeskind's zinc-clad zigzag, opened in 2001, holds the largest Jewish museum in Europe, telling the history of Jews in Germany. The building has no entrance of its own: you go in through the Baroque building next door and down underground. Inside, empty spaces called voids cut through the zigzag; most can be seen but not entered. In the Memory Void you walk over thousands of steel faces by the artist Menashe Kadishman. More than eleven million people visited in its first 16 years.

name: Turning Torso
clues: Nine five-storey cubes twist through 90 degrees up a 190-metre tower, across a narrow strait from a Nordic capital. It began as its architect's sculpture of a human body.
blurb: Santiago Calatrava designed this 190 m apartment tower in Malmö, opened in 2005, from his sculpture of a twisting human body. It is built from nine cubes of five floors each, every one turned a little further than the one below, so the top floor is a full quarter turn from the bottom. When it opened it was the tallest building in Scandinavia, and it kept the Nordic record until 2022. It holds 147 apartments, and on clear days you can see across the strait to Copenhagen.

name: Bosco Verticale
clues: Two apartment towers with around 900 trees on their balconies: a forest stood on end in a fashion capital at the foot of the Alps.
blurb: Designed by Stefano Boeri's studio and finished in 2014, these two towers in Milan carry hundreds of trees and thousands of shrubs and plants on their balconies, more than 90 species in all. The greenery filters dust, absorbs CO2, shades the flats and attracts birds and insects. Before planting, the trees were grown in a nursery and tested in wind tunnels. Arborists abseil down the facades to prune them. In 2015 it was named the most beautiful and innovative skyscraper in the world.

name: Shwedagon Pagoda
clues: A 99-metre gilded stupa on a hill above a Southeast Asian river city. Its tip is set with thousands of diamonds, and it is said to hold strands of the Buddha's hair.
blurb: Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist site, the gilded stupa rises 112 m on a hill above Yangon and is believed to hold relics of four Buddhas, including eight hairs of Gautama Buddha. Tradition says it is more than 2,500 years old; historians date it to between the 6th and 10th centuries. Its outer layer is real gold, and its tip is set with thousands of diamonds and rubies, crowned by a single 76-carat diamond. City rules cap building heights so that it always dominates the skyline.

name: Hassan II Mosque
clues: Its 210-metre minaret is one of the tallest in the world. Part of the prayer hall stands over the Atlantic on Africa's north-west coast, and the roof slides open.
blurb: Completed in 1993 to designs by Michel Pinseau, it stands on a promontory over the Atlantic in Casablanca, and worshippers can pray above the sea. Its minaret is 210 m tall, one of the tallest in the world, and a laser at the top points towards Mecca. It holds about 25,000 worshippers inside and 80,000 more on the esplanade. Some 3,300 Moroccan craftsmen worked on its carved wood, plaster and zellige tilework, and the roof of the prayer hall slides open.

name: Zeitz MOCAA
wiki: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa
clues: Galleries carved out of the 42 concrete tubes of an old grain silo on a harbour waterfront.
Once the tallest building in sub-Saharan Africa, an old grain silo now shows contemporary art, its bulging pillow windows glowing at night by a harbour under a flat-topped mountain.
blurb: This Cape Town museum opened in 2017 inside a grain silo from 1921 that was once the tallest building in sub-Saharan Africa. Thomas Heatherwick's studio carved its atrium out of the silo's 42 concrete tubes in the shape of a single grain of corn, enlarged to fill the space. It is the largest museum of contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. The pillow-shaped windows of the upper floors bulge outwards and glow like lanterns at night.

name: Transitional Cathedral (Cardboard Cathedral)
clues: A church built from giant cardboard tubes after an earthquake wrecked the city's old cathedral. Meant to be temporary, still standing.
A Japanese architect famous for building with paper tubes made this A-frame church as a stopgap after an earthquake, in a South Pacific city known for its English-style gardens.
blurb: After the 2011 earthquake badly damaged Christchurch's cathedral, the Japanese architect Shigeru Ban designed this temporary replacement, which opened in 2013. Its A-frame is made of about 90 large cardboard tubes resting on shipping containers. The cardboard is coated with waterproof polyurethane and fire retardant, and a polycarbonate roof keeps out the rain. Built as a stopgap, it was designed to last about 50 years. The triangular stained-glass window at the front reuses images from the old cathedral's rose window.

name: Yoyogi National Gymnasium
clues: Swooping roofs hung from steel cables like a suspension bridge, built for the swimming at the first Olympic Games held in Asia.
blurb: Kenzo Tange designed it for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, where it hosted swimming and diving; at the 2020 Games it held handball. Its sweeping roof hangs from two thick steel cables slung between concrete masts, like a suspension bridge, leaving a huge space inside without a single column. The curving shapes also recall the roofs of traditional Japanese temples. It is one of the best-known works of modern Japanese architecture, and Tange went on to win the Pritzker Prize in 1987.

name: White House
clues: Painted sandstone walls give this house its name, and every president of its country has lived here since 1800. British troops set it on fire in 1814.
blurb: The Irish-born architect James Hoban won the design competition and modelled the house on Leinster House in Dublin, today home to the Irish parliament. Built between 1792 and 1800 from Aquia Creek sandstone painted white, it has housed every US president since John Adams. British troops set it on fire in 1814, during the War of 1812, and it had to be rebuilt. Thomas Jefferson added the low colonnades on each wing to hide the stables and storage. Its name is also shorthand for the presidency itself.

name: St Peter's Basilica
architect: Bramante, Michelangelo, Carlo Maderno and Gian Lorenzo Bernini
clues: Michelangelo's dome crowns the largest church on Earth, at the heart of the world's smallest country, while a colonnade opens in front of it like two embracing arms.
blurb: It replaced a fourth-century basilica built by Emperor Constantine, which had grown old and unsafe. Building began in 1506 and took 120 years, passing through the hands of Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, who added the long nave and the front. Michelangelo designed the great dome but died before it was finished. Bernini later shaped the vast oval piazza, its colonnades meant to embrace visitors like the arms of the church. Tradition holds that Saint Peter is buried beneath the high altar.

name: Palace of Versailles
architect: Louis Le Vau, Jules Hardouin-Mansart and André Le Nôtre
clues: A Hall of Mirrors in a palace built to glorify the Sun King, just outside a great capital. The royal court lived here until an angry crowd marched out from the city in 1789.
blurb: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into the grandest palace in Europe, to glorify the monarchy and keep the nobles close where he could watch them. The king, the court and the government lived here from 1682 until October 1789, when a crowd marched from Paris and forced the royal family back to the capital. Le Vau, Hardouin-Mansart and the garden designer Le Nôtre created the ensemble, including the dazzling Hall of Mirrors. Courts all over Europe copied its style. Today it is a museum and one of the most visited sites in France.

name: Cologne Cathedral
architect: Master Gerhard; completed by Ernst Friedrich Zwirner
clues: Twin lacy spires, the tallest of any cathedral, tower beside a busy railway station on the Rhine. Work stopped for nearly 300 years, with a medieval crane left standing on top.
blurb: Building began in 1248 to house relics believed to be those of the Three Kings, but work stopped around 1560 with the church half finished. For centuries a medieval crane stood on the unfinished south tower as part of the skyline. Interest in Gothic revived in the 19th century, and the cathedral was completed to its original medieval plan in 1880. At 157 m its twin spires make it the tallest cathedral in the world. It is Germany's most visited landmark, with about 6 million visitors a year.

name: Willis Tower
architect: Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill)
clues: Black steel tubes bundled together, stepping back as they climb above a windy lakeside city. High up, glass boxes stick out from the wall so visitors can stand over thin air.
blurb: Still widely called the Sears Tower, it opened in 1973 as the tallest building in the world, a title it held for nearly 25 years. Architect Bruce Graham and engineer Fazlur Khan of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill bundled square steel tubes together and stopped them at different heights, which gives the tower its stepped outline. It is 442 m tall, with 110 storeys. More than 1.7 million visitors a year ride up to the Skydeck, the highest observation deck in the United States, where glass boxes jut out from the building.

name: Buckingham Palace
clues: A royal family waves from its balcony, and guards in tall bearskin hats change shift at the gates. It began as a duke's townhouse at the end of a long avenue.
blurb: It began in 1703 as a large townhouse for the Duke of Buckingham. George III bought it in 1761 for Queen Charlotte, and in the early 19th century John Nash and Edward Blore enlarged it with three wings around a courtyard. Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live here, from 1837, and a new east front with the famous balcony later closed off the courtyard. Today it is the monarch's official London home and office, and its forecourt hosts the Changing of the Guard.

name: One World Trade Center
clues: The tallest tower in its hemisphere reaches exactly 1,776 feet, after the year its nation declared independence, at the southern tip of a famous island.
blurb: Designed by David Childs of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it is the main building of the rebuilt World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan, and it opened in 2014. It takes its name from the North Tower of the original complex, destroyed in the attacks of 11 September 2001. Its spire reaches 1,776 feet (541 m), a number chosen for the year of American independence, making it the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere. Its square base turns into eight tall glass triangles as it rises, ending in a square turned 45 degrees.

name: Windsor Castle
clues: Monarchs have lived here for over 900 years, longer than in any other palace in Europe. Its round tower crowns a hill above the Thames, a short ride west of a great capital.
blurb: William the Conqueror built the first castle here in the 11th century, soon after the Norman invasion, to guard the western approach to London. Monarchs have used it since Henry I, making it the longest-occupied palace in Europe. Inside the walls stands the 15th-century St George's Chapel, one of the masterpieces of English Gothic. The lavish state apartments were remodelled in the early 19th century for George IV. A fire in 1992 damaged more than 100 rooms, which were restored over the next five years.

name: Great Mosque of Mecca
architect: Unknown builders, enlarged by many rulers
clues: The largest mosque on Earth surrounds a cube draped in black cloth, and millions of pilgrims walk around it each year, in a desert valley near the Red Sea.
blurb: It is the holiest mosque in Islam and the largest in the world. At its centre stands the Kaaba, the cube draped in black cloth that Muslims everywhere face when they pray, and which tradition says Abraham built. The mosque has been enlarged many times by caliphs, sultans and kings, most dramatically in the 20th and 21st centuries. During the Hajj, millions of pilgrims walk around the Kaaba seven times. Its guardian is the King of Saudi Arabia, who carries the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques.

name: British Museum
architect: Robert Smirke; Great Court by Foster and Partners
clues: A Greek-temple front of columns in a leafy literary district opens onto eight million objects, from the Rosetta Stone to mummies, around a courtyard roofed in a glass lattice.
blurb: Founded in 1753 on the collection of the physician Sir Hans Sloane, it was the world's first public national museum, opening in 1759 in Montagu House. Robert Smirke's Greek Revival building replaced the old house in the 19th century, behind a grand row of Ionic columns. In 2000 Norman Foster covered its inner courtyard with a roof of glass and steel, creating the Great Court. Its collection of about eight million objects, the Rosetta Stone among them, is the largest of its kind. Many were acquired during the British Empire, which keeps debates about returning them alive.

name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
architect: Calvert Vaux, Richard Morris Hunt and others
clues: A Beaux-Arts palace of art on the edge of a huge urban park, whose grand front steps fill with celebrities in outrageous outfits every May for a famous fashion gala.
blurb: The largest art museum in the Americas, it holds well over a million works in 17 departments, from an Egyptian temple to modern painting. Its main building sits on Fifth Avenue at the eastern edge of Central Park. The first part, opened in 1880, is now hidden inside later wings, and Richard Morris Hunt designed the grand Beaux-Arts front on Fifth Avenue. More than five million people visited in 2025. Each May its steps host the Met Gala, one of the most photographed nights in fashion.

name: United States Capitol
architect: William Thornton; dome by Thomas U. Walter
clues: A white cast-iron dome tops the hall where a nation's lawmakers meet, at one end of a long grassy mall. The city's street numbers all count outward from here.
blurb: William Thornton's design won the competition in 1793, and Congress first met here in November 1800, after the capital moved from Philadelphia. British troops set it on fire in 1814, and it was restored within a few years. The famous dome is not stone but cast iron painted white, added by Thomas U. Walter in the 1850s and 1860s, and finished during the Civil War. The building is also the starting point for the city's street numbers and its four quadrants. It stands at the eastern end of the National Mall.

name: St Paul's Cathedral
clues: A great Baroque dome raised after a fire burned a city's old cathedral down. Whisper against the wall of the gallery inside and someone on the far side can hear you.
blurb: Old St Paul's was largely destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666, and Christopher Wren was given the job of rebuilding it. His English Baroque cathedral was finished in 1710 on Ludgate Hill, the highest point in the City of London. Its dome, inspired by St Peter's in Rome, is one of the largest in the world and ruled the skyline for centuries. Inside, the Whispering Gallery carries a quiet voice all the way round the dome. Wren himself is buried in the crypt.

name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
wiki: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
clues: A glass pyramid leaning against a white tower on a Great Lakes shore, designed by the architect of the Louvre's pyramid, honours the loudest music of the 20th century.
blurb: Atlantic Records founder Ahmet Ertegun set up the Hall of Fame foundation in 1983, and after a long search Cleveland was chosen as its home in 1986. The city had a good claim: the local DJ Alan Freed helped popularise the term 'rock and roll'. I. M. Pei designed the museum, a glass pyramid leaning against a tower on the shore of Lake Erie, and it opened in 1995. Inside, it tells the story of rock through guitars, stage costumes and handwritten lyrics. New members are inducted every year.

name: Milan Cathedral
clues: A forest of white marble spires and thousands of statues, begun in 1386 and only finished in 1965. Visitors stroll across its roof in a northern fashion capital.
blurb: Construction began in 1386, and the last details were only completed in 1965, almost six centuries later. It is the largest church in Italy, since the bigger St Peter's is in Vatican City. It is built of pinkish-white marble from Candoglia, once brought down to the city by canal. Its roof bristles with spires and thousands of statues, and visitors can walk across its terraces among the pinnacles. On the highest spire stands the Madonnina, a gilded statue of the Virgin Mary and a symbol of the city.

name: Tokyo Skytree
clues: The tallest tower in the world, a white steel lattice 634 m high, its base a triangle that turns into a circle as it rises over a vast Asian capital.
blurb: Completed on 29 February 2012 and opened that May, it is 634 m tall, the tallest tower in the world and the third-tallest structure. The number was chosen on purpose: read in Japanese as 'mu-sa-shi', it recalls Musashi, the old name of the region. It was built because high-rises had begun to block signals from the older Tokyo Tower, and it is now the main broadcast site for the Kantō region. Its base is a triangle that becomes a circle as it rises. Two observation decks sit at 350 m and 450 m.

name: Florence Cathedral
architect: Arnolfo di Cambio; dome by Filippo Brunelleschi
clues: Green, pink and white marble outside, and a huge brick dome that nobody knew how to build, until a goldsmith worked it out. A Tuscan Renaissance puzzle in stone.
blurb: Begun in 1296 to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, the cathedral waited decades for a dome nobody knew how to build. Filippo Brunelleschi, trained as a goldsmith, won the competition and completed it in 1436 without the usual wooden framework, using bricks laid in a herringbone pattern and two shells, one inside the other. It is still the largest brick dome in the world. The outside is faced in green, pink and white marble, and the west front was only finished in the 19th century. Giotto's bell tower and the Baptistery stand beside it.

name: Reichstag
architect: Paul Wallot; rebuilt by Norman Foster
clues: Visitors climb a spiral ramp inside a glass dome and look straight down on the lawmakers below, in a 19th-century parliament beside a river in a once-divided capital.
blurb: Paul Wallot's Neo-Renaissance building opened in 1894 for the parliament of the German Empire. A fire in 1933 gutted it and helped the Nazis tighten their grip on power, and the war left it a ruin. After reunification, Norman Foster rebuilt it for the Bundestag, which moved in in 1999. His glass dome has a mirrored cone in the middle that reflects daylight down into the chamber, and visitors walk up a spiral ramp above the politicians' heads. In 1995 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the whole building in silver fabric.

name: Winter Palace
clues: A mint-green and white Baroque palace of 1,500 rooms on a wide northern river, home to the tsars and now part of one of the world's greatest art museums.
blurb: The present palace, the fourth on the site, was designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli and largely finished in 1762. It was the official residence of the Russian emperors until 1917. It is said to contain 1,500 rooms, 1,945 windows and 117 staircases. After a fire in 1837 it was quickly rebuilt. The storming of the palace in 1917, retold in Soviet paintings and in Eisenstein's film October, became a symbol of the revolution. Today it is part of the State Hermitage Museum.

name: Topkapı Palace
clues: Sultans ran an empire from these courtyards for nearly 400 years, on a hilly point where the Golden Horn meets a strait between two continents.
blurb: Sultan Mehmed II ordered it built in 1459, six years after conquering Constantinople. For almost four centuries it was the centre of Ottoman government and the main home of the sultans, until they moved to Dolmabahçe Palace in 1853. Rather than one huge building, it is a series of four courtyards with pavilions, kitchens, a treasury and the harem, where the sultan's family lived. Its name, meaning Cannon Gate, was only given in the 19th century. Today it is a museum full of relics, jewels and manuscripts.

name: Red Fort
clues: Red sandstone walls of a Mughal emperor's citadel, where the prime minister raises the national flag every Independence Day, in a huge capital on the Yamuna.
blurb: Emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it in 1639 when he moved the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi, and it was finished in 1648. Its design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who is also credited with the Taj Mahal. Inside the red sandstone walls stood marble palaces, audience halls and gardens, blending Persian and Indian styles. Nadir Shah's army plundered it in 1739, and after 1857 the British demolished many of its buildings. Every year on 15 August, the Prime Minister of India raises the flag here and speaks to the nation.

name: Sultan Ahmed Mosque (Blue Mosque)
clues: Six minarets and a cascade of domes, with thousands of blue tiles inside that gave it its nickname. It faces an older domed giant across a square where chariots once raced.
blurb: Sultan Ahmed I built it between 1609 and 1617, beside the old Hippodrome and facing Hagia Sophia. Its architect, Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, was a pupil of the great Sinan. A central dome rests on four half-domes, and the interior is lined with thousands of Iznik tiles and painted flowers in mostly blue tones, which gave it its popular name. It is unusual for having six minarets. The complex also includes Ahmed's tomb and a madrasa, and it is still a working mosque.

name: Makkah Royal Clock Tower
clues: The largest timepiece dials ever made glow from a 600-metre tower in a desert city, looming over the courtyard that millions of pilgrims travel to each year.
blurb: The central tower of this seven-tower hotel complex is about 601 m tall, one of the tallest buildings in the world, and Guinness lists it as the tallest clock tower. Its four clock faces are the largest ever built. The government built the complex to house pilgrims right next to the Great Mosque, with design led by the firm Dar Al-Handasah. It is among the most expensive buildings ever made. Building it meant demolishing an Ottoman-era fortress on the hill, which drew protests from Turkey.

name: Shanghai Tower
clues: A glass skyscraper twisting a third of a turn as it climbs 632 m, the tallest in its country, standing beside two famous neighbours on the riverbank of a huge port city.
blurb: Designed by Gensler, it stands 632 m tall in the Lujiazui financial district, next to the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest in the world. The tower twists about 120 degrees as it rises, a shape that reduces the wind load on the building. Two glass skins wrap around it, with sky gardens in the space between. Its lifts were the fastest in the world until 2017, at 20.5 m per second.

name: Burj Al Arab
clues: A hotel shaped like a billowing sail on its own artificial island, with a helipad jutting out near the top, just off a beach on the Gulf.
blurb: Designed by Tom Wright of Atkins and opened in 1999, it is one of the tallest hotels in the world, although 39% of its height is empty space. It stands on an artificial island 280 m off Jumeirah Beach, joined to the shore by a private curving bridge. Its shape copies the sail of a dhow, a traditional Arab boat. Near the roof, 210 m up, a helipad has hosted a tennis match and a golf drive. It became the symbol of the city's boom.

name: Schönbrunn Palace
architect: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and Nicolò Pacassi
clues: A 1,441-room summer palace painted in its very own shade of yellow, home of an imperial dynasty, with the world's oldest zoo in its garden, on the edge of a waltzing capital.
blurb: Its name means 'beautiful spring', after an artesian well whose water was drunk by the court. The Habsburgs used it as their main summer residence, and its Baroque form largely dates from the 18th century, designed by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and later reworked by Nicolò Pacassi for Empress Maria Theresa. Its 1,441 rooms sit behind walls in a colour so typical it is called Schönbrunn yellow. The gardens hold the oldest zoo in the world still running, founded in 1752. It has drawn crowds of tourists since the 1950s.

name: Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba
architect: Commissioned by Abd al-Rahman I; cathedral nave by Hernán Ruiz
clues: A forest of hundreds of columns under red-and-white striped arches, with a Renaissance cathedral built right into the middle of it, in a hot Andalusian city.
blurb: Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Emirate of Córdoba, ordered the Great Mosque built in 785, and it was enlarged several times over the next two centuries. Its prayer hall is a forest of columns topped with double arches striped in red brick and white stone. After Christian forces took the city in 1236, it became a cathedral. In the 16th century a Renaissance nave was built right in the middle of the hall. Emperor Charles V is said to have regretted it, saying they had destroyed something unique to build something ordinary.

name: Tokyo Tower
clues: An orange-and-white lattice tower modelled on a famous Parisian one, and a little taller, glowing over a giant Asian capital at night.
blurb: Completed in 1958, the lattice tower was inspired by the Eiffel Tower and stands 332.9 m tall. It is painted white and international orange to meet air safety rules, and repainting it every five years takes about a year. It was the tallest tower in Japan until Tokyo Skytree took over in 2012, partly because new high-rises had begun to block its television signals. Visitors can go up to a main deck at 150 m and a top deck at about 250 m. At its foot, a five-storey building holds shops and restaurants.

name: Castel Sant'Angelo
clues: A Roman emperor's round tomb beside the Tiber, later a papal fortress joined to the Vatican by a raised escape passage, with a bronze angel on top.
blurb: Emperor Hadrian built this huge cylinder as a mausoleum for himself and his family, and it was finished around 139 AD. For a time it was the tallest building in Rome. The popes later turned it into a fortress and linked it to the Vatican by the Passetto, a raised, walled passage they could flee along in times of danger. Its name comes from a legend that the Archangel Michael appeared above it in 590 to end a plague. A bronze statue of the angel stands on top, and today it is a museum.

name: Jerónimos Monastery
architect: Diogo de Boitaca and João de Castilho
clues: Stone carved with ropes, sea creatures and armillary spheres, paid for with spice-trade riches, near where an explorer set sail for India from a wide Atlantic river mouth.
blurb: It was built from the early 1500s near the spot where Vasco da Gama set off on his first voyage to India, and paid for by a tax on the profits of the spice trade. It is the finest example of the Manueline style, a late Portuguese Gothic full of carved ropes, shells, plants and armillary spheres celebrating the age of exploration. Monks of the Order of Saint Jerome lived here until 1833. In 1880 da Gama's remains were moved here, along with those of the poet Luís de Camões. Several kings are buried here too.

name: York Minster
clues: Its great east window holds more medieval stained glass than any other in the land. A Gothic giant inside old Roman and medieval walls, in the north of England.
blurb: A church has stood here since at least 627, but the Gothic building was raised between 1220 and 1472. It is the seat of the Archbishop of York, the second-highest office in the Church of England. Its Great East Window, glazed in the early 1400s, is the largest area of medieval stained glass in the country. The minster mixes several stages of Gothic, from the Early English transepts to the Perpendicular east end. In 1984 lightning set the south transept roof on fire, and the heat cracked the rose window.

name: Prambanan
architect: Unknown builders of the Mataram kingdom
clues: Sharp stone towers, the tallest 47 m high, honour a Hindu trinity on a mostly Muslim island, between a smoking volcano and an old royal city.
blurb: Built in the 9th century, it is the largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia and second only to Angkor Wat in Southeast Asia. It is dedicated to the Trimurti: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer. The central Shiva temple rises 47 m, ringed by smaller shrines; the compound once held 240 temples. Carvings on its walls tell the Ramayana, which is also danced as a ballet on an open-air stage nearby. Earthquakes have damaged it several times, and restoration still goes on.

name: Basilica of San Vitale
clues: An eight-sided brick church whose plain outside hides glittering gold mosaics of a Byzantine emperor and empress, in a former imperial capital near the Adriatic.
blurb: Consecrated in 547, this sixth-century church is one of the best-preserved works of early Byzantine art. Its plain brick exterior gives no hint of the inside, which is planned around an octagon and covered in mosaics. The most famous show Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora with their courts, shimmering in gold and green. Ravenna had been the capital of the Western Roman Empire and later a Byzantine stronghold in Italy. It is one of eight buildings in the city on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

name: Bolshoi Theatre
architect: Joseph Bové; rebuilt by Albert Cavos
clues: Eight white columns and Apollo driving a bronze chariot crown the front of a famous ballet house, home to more than 200 dancers, in a snowy capital.
blurb: The company dates from 1776, and the present building was designed by Joseph Bové and opened in 1825. After a fire in 1853 Albert Cavos rebuilt it, keeping the portico of eight columns crowned by Apollo driving a four-horse chariot. The Bolshoi Ballet is the largest ballet company in the world, with more than 200 dancers, and its name simply means 'big'. A six-year restoration finished in 2011 brought back the original acoustics and decoration. The building appears on the 100-rouble banknote.

name: Tōdai-ji
clues: One of the largest wooden buildings in the world shelters a giant bronze Buddha, while tame deer wander outside bowing for crackers, in an old capital.
blurb: Emperor Shōmu founded it in the 8th century, and it opened in 752, modelled on the great temples of Tang China. Its Great Buddha Hall shelters a bronze Buddha about 15 m tall. The present hall dates from 1709 and is smaller than the original, yet it is still one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. By the late 19th century its heavy roof was close to collapse, and a restoration from 1904 to 1913 saved it. Outside, hundreds of sika deer roam freely and bow for crackers.

name: Dolby Theatre
clues: Every year the film world's best-known golden statuettes are handed out here, inside a shopping mall on a boulevard paved with stars, in a sunny Pacific city.
blurb: Opened in November 2001 as the Kodak Theatre, it was designed by David Rockwell specially to host the Academy Awards, which have been held here ever since. It sits inside the Ovation Hollywood shopping and entertainment complex on Hollywood Boulevard, next to the TCL Chinese Theatre with its famous footprints in cement. Kodak's name came off in 2012 after the company went bankrupt, and Dolby took over. Between Oscar nights it hosts concerts and shows.

name: Palace of Fontainebleau
clues: A royal hunting lodge in a great forest south of a capital, where a defeated emperor said goodbye to his guard at the foot of a horseshoe staircase.
blurb: For eight centuries French rulers, from Louis VII to Napoleon III, came here to hunt in the surrounding forest, about 55 km southeast of Paris. Francis I turned the medieval lodge into a Renaissance palace, bringing in Italian artists who founded what became known as the School of Fontainebleau. Napoleon loved it and called it 'the true home of kings'. In 1814, after his abdication, he said farewell to his Old Guard in the courtyard below the horseshoe-shaped staircase. It became a national museum in 1927.

name: Stirling Castle
clues: A royal castle on a cliff-ringed crag guarding the lowest crossing of a Scottish river, where a queen was crowned at nine months old.
blurb: It sits on a crag of hard rock with cliffs on three sides, guarding what was until the 1890s the lowest crossing of the River Forth. Whoever held it controlled the way into the Highlands, so it was besieged many times. Most of the main buildings date from the 15th and 16th centuries, when it was a favourite home of the Stuart kings. Mary, Queen of Scots, was crowned in its chapel in 1543 at just nine months old. The battles of Stirling Bridge and Bannockburn were fought within sight of its walls.

name: Lakhta Centre
clues: Europe's tallest building, a twisting glass spire 462 m high shaped like a flame, on the shore of a Baltic gulf at the edge of a northern city of canals.
blurb: At 462 m it is the tallest building in Russia and in Europe, and the northernmost skyscraper in the world. Designed by RMJM for the energy company Gazprom, it was built from 2012 and topped out in 2018. Its five wings twist as they rise to a spire, a shape meant to recall a flame. It stands on the shore of the Gulf of Finland, far from the historic centre, after an earlier plan to build a tower closer in drew protests over the skyline. Its top floors hold a public observation deck.

name: Palazzo Pitti
architect: Attributed to Filippo Brunelleschi; built by Luca Fancelli
clues: A banker built this rough-stone palace to outshine his rivals, and then his rivals bought it. It stands across a Tuscan river from an old bridge lined with jewellers' shops.
blurb: The core of the palace was built from 1458 for Luca Pitti, an ambitious banker who wanted a home grander than the Medici's. The design is often attributed to Brunelleschi, with Luca Fancelli building it. In 1549 the Medici bought it themselves, and it became the main residence of the Grand Dukes of Tuscany. They laid out the Boboli Gardens behind it and filled it with treasures. Napoleon later used it as a base, and it was briefly a royal palace when Florence was the capital of Italy. Today it holds several museums.

name: Pashupatinath Temple
clues: A Shiva temple with a gilded double roof beside a sacred river where open-air cremations burn day and night, in a Himalayan valley.
blurb: Dedicated to Pashupati, a form of Shiva, it is one of the holiest Hindu sites in South Asia. The main temple, with its two-tiered gilded roof and silver doors, stands on the banks of the Bagmati River, and only Hindus may enter it. Around it a vast precinct of shrines, ashrams and images has grown up over the centuries. On stone platforms along the river, cremations take place in the open. It has been part of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site since 1979.

name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
clues: A royal palace at the bottom of a cobbled mile, facing a castle on a rock at the top, between a ruined abbey and an old volcano in a northern capital.
blurb: It is the monarch's official residence in Scotland, at the opposite end of the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle. It grew from the guest house of Holyrood Abbey, whose roofless ruins still stand beside it, and has been the main royal home in Scotland since the 16th century. Mary, Queen of Scots, lived here, and her secretary David Rizzio was murdered in her private rooms in 1566. Much of the palace was rebuilt in the 1670s for Charles II, to designs by Sir William Bruce. The King spends a week here each summer.

name: Kailasa Temple, Ellora
architect: Commissioned by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I
clues: Not built up but carved downward out of a single basalt hillside: a whole multi-storey temple to Shiva in the dry basalt hills of the Deccan plateau.
blurb: This temple was not built from stones but carved out of the rock: workers cut down into a basalt hillside and removed a vast amount of stone to free a complete temple. It was made in the 8th century and is usually credited to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. The tower over the sanctuary rises 32.6 m above the courtyard. It is dedicated to Shiva and named after Mount Kailash, his home in the Himalayas. It is the largest of the 34 Hindu, Buddhist and Jain cave temples at Ellora.

name: Palace of Culture and Science
clues: A wedding-cake tower given by Stalin to a central European capital on the Vistula. Locals joked its viewing deck had the best view in town, because from there you can't see it.
blurb: Designed by the Soviet architect Lev Rudnev and finished in 1955, it was a gift from the Soviet Union, in the style of Moscow's 'Seven Sisters' skyscrapers. Rudnev mixed in details from Polish Renaissance buildings and American Art Deco. At 237 m it was one of the tallest buildings in the world when it opened, and it stayed the tallest in Poland until 2022. It holds theatres, cinemas, museums and offices. Many Poles disliked it as a symbol of Soviet rule, but it has become a landmark of the city.

name: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest)
clues: White temples cling to a sheer cliff high above a Himalayan valley, where legend says a guru flew in on the back of a tigress to meditate in a cave.
blurb: The monastery was built in 1692 around a cave, clinging to a cliff high above the Paro valley. Legend says Guru Padmasambhava, who brought Vajrayana Buddhism to the region, flew here on the back of a tigress more than a thousand years ago and meditated in the cave. It is the best known of thirteen 'tiger's lair' caves linked to him. Reaching it takes a steep walk of a couple of hours. A fire in 1998 destroyed much of the main building, and it was carefully restored.

name: Kunsthistorisches Museum
architect: Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer
clues: An emperor built twin palaces, one for art and one for nature, facing each other across a square on a grand ring road. This one holds his dynasty's paintings under an eight-sided dome.
blurb: Emperor Franz Joseph opened it in 1891 to house the vast art collections of the Habsburgs. Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer designed it as one of a pair of matching museums on the Ringstrasse, facing the Natural History Museum across Maria-Theresien-Platz. An octagonal dome crowns the building, and the paintings above the grand staircase include work by a young Gustav Klimt. It is the largest art museum in Austria, famous for its paintings by Bruegel, Vermeer, Raphael and Velázquez.

name: Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral
clues: Built on top of an Aztec sacred precinct beside a vast square, this huge cathedral has been sinking unevenly into the soft clay of a drained lake.
blurb: Spanish builders began it in 1573 on top of the sacred precinct of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, next to the remains of the Templo Mayor. It took until 1813 to finish, so it mixes Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles. Claudio de Arciniega drew the first plans, inspired by cathedrals in Spain. It stands on the north side of the Zócalo, one of the largest city squares in the world. Because the city sits on soft clay from a former lake, the cathedral sinks unevenly, and major engineering work in the 1990s stabilised it.

name: Landmark 81
clues: Glass tubes of different heights bundled like bamboo stems rise 461 m beside a river in the biggest city of a long, narrow Southeast Asian country.
blurb: Completed in 2018, it is the tallest building in Vietnam at 461 m, with 81 storeys. The design by Atkins is said to be inspired by a bundle of bamboo stems, a traditional symbol of unity and strength, with glass tubes rising to different heights. It stands on the bank of the Saigon River next to Saigon Bridge, on the site of an old logistics base. The tower holds a hotel, flats, offices, shops and an observation deck near the top. It is the centrepiece of a large riverside development by Vinhomes.

name: Vaduz Castle
clues: A prince still lives in this medieval castle on a terrace above the Rhine, looking down on the capital of one of Europe's tiniest countries, tucked between two Alpine neighbours.
blurb: It is the palace and home of the Prince of Liechtenstein, perched high above the capital, which took its name from the castle. Its oldest parts are medieval, and it was largely restored in the early 20th century. Prince Franz Joseph II moved in for good in 1938, the first ruling prince to live in the country. The castle is not open to the public, but on the national holiday, 15 August, people are invited into the garden. It looks across the Rhine valley to Switzerland.

name: Etchmiadzin Cathedral
architect: Founded by Saint Gregory the Illuminator
clues: Often called the oldest cathedral in the world, founded soon after a Caucasus kingdom became the first to adopt Christianity, within sight of a snowy biblical mountain.
blurb: Tradition says Saint Gregory the Illuminator built the first church here between 301 and 303, after King Tiridates III made Armenia the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion. It was built over a pagan temple, and it is often called the oldest cathedral in the world. The core of today's building dates from 483 or 484, after a Persian invasion badly damaged the church. It is the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church and the seat of its head, the Catholicos. Its cone-topped domes are typical of Armenian architecture.

name: Art Institute of Chicago
architect: Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge; Modern Wing by Renzo Piano
clues: Two bronze lions guard the steps of this art museum by a great lake, where you can stand before American Gothic and a lonely late-night diner.
blurb: Founded in 1879, it moved into its Beaux-Arts building in Grant Park in 1893, the year of the World's Columbian Exposition. Two bronze lions by Edward Kemeys guard the entrance on Michigan Avenue. Its collection of nearly 300,000 works includes Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Edward Hopper's Nighthawks and Grant Wood's American Gothic. In 2009 Renzo Piano added the light-filled Modern Wing. It is one of the oldest and largest art museums in the United States.

name: Buda Castle
clues: A green-domed royal palace on a hilltop, reached by a little funicular, above a great river that splits a central European capital in two.
blurb: Hungarian kings first built a castle on this hill in the 13th century. The Baroque palace that fills most of the site went up between 1749 and 1769 and was later greatly expanded by Miklós Ybl and Alajos Hauszmann. It was badly damaged in the Siege of Budapest in the Second World War and rebuilt in a simpler style under communist rule. Today it holds the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library. A funicular climbs up to it from the Danube.

name: Basilica of Santa Croce
clues: Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli all lie in this Franciscan church, on a square where a Tuscan city still plays a brutal historic football match.
blurb: The main Franciscan church of Florence was begun in 1294, possibly to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, and consecrated in 1442. It was built on marshland outside the old city walls. So many famous Italians are buried or remembered here, among them Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli and Rossini, that it is called the Temple of the Italian Glories. Inside are frescoes by Giotto. Its marble front was only added in the 19th century. In the square outside, the city still plays its rough historic football, calcio storico.

name: John Hancock Center (875 North Michigan Avenue)
architect: Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill)
clues: Giant X-braces criss-cross the dark sides of this tapering 100-storey tower, where a viewing deck tilts visitors out over a busy avenue by a great lake.
blurb: Still widely known as the John Hancock Center, it was designed by Bruce Graham and engineer Fazlur Khan of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and topped out in 1968. When finished it was the second-tallest building in the world, after the Empire State Building. Its huge diagonal X-braces are part of the structure: they turn the outside into a stiff tube and saved a great deal of steel. The 100-storey tower tapers as it rises and mixes offices, flats and restaurants. On the 94th floor, a ride called Tilt leans visitors out over Michigan Avenue.

name: Lotte World Tower
clues: A smooth white-glass cone 555 m tall, said to echo traditional ceramics and a calligraphy brush, rising beside a lake and a theme park in an East Asian capital.
blurb: Opened in April 2017, it is 555 m tall with 123 floors, the tallest building in South Korea and among the tallest in the world. Kohn Pedersen Fox shaped it as a smooth, gently tapering cone, inspired by Korean ceramics and the curve of a calligraphy brush. A seam runs up its side, pointing towards the old city centre. Near the top, a glass-floored observatory looks over the city, and a 'Sky Bridge Tour' lets visitors walk across the roof itself. It stands beside the Lotte World theme park and Seokchon Lake.

name: Barcelona Cathedral
clues: Thirteen white geese live in the cloister of this Gothic cathedral, one for each year of a young martyr's life, in the old quarter of a Mediterranean port.
blurb: Built mainly in the 14th century, it is the seat of the Archbishop of Barcelona and stands in the heart of the Gothic Quarter. Its cloister, finished in 1448, holds the Well of the Geese, where thirteen white geese are kept, said to stand for the age of Saint Eulalia when she was martyred. She is buried in the crypt. The ornate neo-Gothic front was only added in the late 19th century, over the plain exterior typical of Catalan churches. A lift takes visitors up to the roof.

name: Amiens Cathedral
clues: The roomiest Gothic cathedral in its country, built in about fifty years, its carved front once painted in bright colours, on a ridge above the Somme.
blurb: Built almost entirely between 1220 and about 1270, a short time for a Gothic cathedral, it has an unusual unity of style. Its first architect was Robert de Luzarches. By interior volume it is the largest cathedral in France, and its nave vault rises about 42 m. Its west front is covered in carved figures, and light shows now project the colours they were once painted in. It came through both world wars largely intact. It stands on a slight ridge above the River Somme, about 120 km north of Paris.

name: El Castillo (Temple of Kukulcán)
clues: A stepped pyramid with 365 steps, where at the equinoxes the afternoon sun draws a shadow serpent sliding down the stairs, in the flat jungle of a big peninsula.
blurb: The great step pyramid dominates the centre of Chichén Itzá, a Maya city at its height around 900 to 1000 AD. It is dedicated to Kukulcán, the feathered serpent god. Each of its four sides has 91 steps, which together with the top platform make 365, one for each day of the year. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the afternoon sun casts triangles of shadow down the northern stairway, like a snake sliding down to the carved serpent heads at the bottom. Inside it, archaeologists found an older pyramid.

name: Dancing House
clues: A glass tower pinched at the waist leans into a stone partner like two dancers, on a riverbank among the Baroque and Art Nouveau of a central European capital.
blurb: Designed by Vlado Milunić with Frank Gehry and finished in 1996, it stands on a riverside plot left empty since an American bombing raid hit it by mistake in 1945. Gehry first nicknamed it Ginger and Fred, after the dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire: the stone tower is Fred, and the pinched glass one is Ginger leaning into him. Its curves caused controversy among the city's historic buildings. Václav Havel, who lived next door, backed the project. Today it holds offices, a hotel, a gallery and a rooftop restaurant.

name: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
clues: A granite temple of art with murals by a famous portrait painter in its rotunda and one of the largest Japanese collections outside Japan, in an old harbour city of New England.
blurb: Founded in 1870 in Copley Square, the museum moved in 1909 to its present building on the Fenway, designed by Guy Lowell with a granite front and a central rotunda. It owns more than 500,000 works and one of the largest collections of Japanese art outside Japan. John Singer Sargent painted the murals of the rotunda and the grand staircase. I. M. Pei added the West Wing in 1981, and Foster and Partners built the glass-roofed Art of the Americas wing in 2010.

name: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
clues: Its wavy, rough stone front made locals nickname it 'the stone quarry', and chimneys like helmeted warriors guard its roof, in a Mediterranean grid of cut-corner blocks.
blurb: It was the last private house designed by Antoni Gaudí, built between 1906 and 1912 for Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon. Its rippling stone front, with hardly a straight line, made locals call it La Pedrera, 'the stone quarry', and it was controversial at the time. The twisted iron balconies were designed by Josep Maria Jujol. The stone façade supports itself, so the floors inside are open and walls could go anywhere, and it even had an underground garage. On the roof, chimneys and air towers look like helmeted warriors.

name: Heidelberg Castle
clues: A red sandstone ruin, wrecked by lightning and by French armies, looming over the old university town in a wooded valley where the Neckar leaves the hills.
blurb: The first castle here was built before 1214 and grew into a grand palace of the Electors Palatine, now among the most important Renaissance buildings north of the Alps. Lightning destroyed the upper castle in 1537, and French troops blew up much of it in wars at the end of the 17th century. Partly rebuilt, it was struck by lightning again in 1764 and left as a ruin. Romantic writers and painters then made the red sandstone ruin famous. In its cellar sits the Heidelberg Tun, one of the largest wine barrels in the world.

name: Tomb of Cyrus the Great
