clues: A simple gabled stone room on six steps holds the founder of a vast ancient empire. Its base has shrugged off earthquakes for 2,500 years on a high plateau north of the Gulf.
blurb: It stands in Pasargadae, the first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BC. The tomb is a small gabled chamber of pale limestone resting on six stepped tiers. It is said to be the oldest base-isolated building in the world: its foundation lets it shift rather than crack, and it has survived many earthquakes. Ancient writers say Alexander the Great visited it and ordered it repaired. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of Pasargadae.

name: Wartburg
clues: Hiding here in disguise, a rebel monk translated the New Testament into his own people's language in about eleven weeks, in a castle on a forested crag in the green heart of central Europe.
blurb: According to legend it was founded in 1067, and it stands on a precipice 410 m up above the town of Eisenach in Thuringia. Saint Elisabeth of Hungary lived here, and in 1521 and 1522 Martin Luther hid here as 'Junker Jörg', translating the New Testament into German. In 1817 students gathered here for the Wartburg Festival, calling for a united Germany. Its romantic 19th-century restoration inspired King Ludwig II when he planned Neuschwanstein. Much of the interior dates from that time, but large medieval parts survive.

name: Museo Reina Sofía
architect: Francesco Sabatini; extension by Jean Nouvel
wiki: Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía
clues: Glass lift towers climb the outside of an 18th-century hospital, where a huge grey canvas of a bombed town hangs, in a high, dry inland capital.
blurb: Spain's national museum of 20th-century art opened in 1992 in a former 18th-century general hospital designed by Francesco Sabatini. Glass lift towers were added to the outside, and in 2005 Jean Nouvel built an extension under a vast red roof. Its most famous work is Picasso's Guernica, painted in 1937 after the bombing of a Basque town in the Spanish Civil War. The collection is strong on Picasso, Dalí and Miró. With the Prado and the Thyssen it forms the city's 'Golden Triangle of Art'.

name: Frauenkirche (Munich Cathedral)
clues: Twin brick towers with rounded green caps set the height limit for a beer-loving city near the Alps, and a footprint by the door is said to be the devil's own.
blurb: Built by Jörg von Halsbach from 1468 and consecrated in 1494, it is the cathedral of Munich and a symbol of the city. Its twin brick towers, about 99 m tall, wear rounded domes added in the 16th century. After a local vote in 2004, new buildings in the centre may not rise higher than them. Near the entrance, a dark footprint in the floor is said to have been left by the Devil, stamping in anger. It is the largest hall church in the world, and it was rebuilt after heavy damage in the Second World War.

name: Conwy Castle
clues: Eight massive round towers raised in just four years by a conquering king, joined to a walled town on a tidal estuary in a mountainous western land.
blurb: Edward I built it between 1283 and 1287 during his conquest of Wales, with Master James of St George as architect. It was part of a project to create the walled town of Conwy, and castle and walls together cost about £15,000, a huge sum at the time. Its eight great towers still stand. The castle survived a siege in the winter of 1294 to 1295, sheltered Richard II in 1399 and held out for the king in the Civil War until 1646. It is part of a World Heritage Site with Edward's other castles in north Wales.

name: Mauritshuis
clues: A small square palace beside a pond, where a girl with a pearl earring gazes out among Golden Age masters, in a seat of government near the North Sea.
blurb: Built for Count John Maurice of Nassau and finished in 1641, the house was designed by Jacob van Campen in a calm Dutch classical style. It stands beside the Hofvijver pond, next to the Binnenhof parliament buildings. Since 1822 it has housed the Royal Cabinet of Paintings, a small collection of about 850 works, mostly from the Dutch Golden Age. Highlights include Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and View of Delft, Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson of Dr Tulp and Fabritius's The Goldfinch.

name: Peace Palace
clues: A Scottish-born steel magnate paid for this neo-Renaissance courthouse, where nations settle quarrels by law, in a seat of government by the North Sea.
blurb: It opened on 28 August 1913 to house the Permanent Court of Arbitration, created by the Hague Convention of 1899 in the hope of ending war through law. Andrew Carnegie paid for it, and Louis Cordonnier won the design competition. Countries sent gifts for the interior, from marble to tapestries and a huge vase from the Tsar of Russia. Since 1946 it has also housed the International Court of Justice, the main court of the United Nations. The First World War broke out less than a year after it opened.

name: Hermann Castle
clues: A medieval fortress with a tall square tower stares across a narrow river at another castle on the far bank, at the very eastern edge of the European Union.
blurb: The castle was founded around 1256, when this area belonged to the Danish crown, and its first full stone walls went up in the early 14th century. The Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order bought it in 1346. Its tall square keep, the Hermann Tower, is the symbol of the town. Across the Narva River stands the Russian fortress of Ivangorod, so two castles face each other across the border. Narva lies on the eastern edge of Estonia and of the European Union.

name: Griffith Observatory
architect: John C. Austin and Frederick M. Ashley
clues: Three copper domes on a dry hillside above a sprawling Pacific basin. More people have looked through its free telescope than through any other in the world.
blurb: Griffith J. Griffith gave the land and left money for it on condition that entry be free, as it has been since it opened in 1935. The Art Deco building on the slope of Mount Hollywood looks out over the city, the Hollywood Sign and the Pacific. More than 9 million people have looked through its 12-inch Zeiss refracting telescope, the most viewed telescope in the world. Inside are a planetarium and exhibits about space. It has appeared in many films, most famously Rebel Without a Cause.

name: Q1 Tower
clues: A slim residential tower of 322 m, its spire inspired by an Olympic torch, the tallest in its country, rising from a surf beach on a sunny eastern coast.
blurb: Opened in November 2005, it was the world's tallest residential building until 2011 and is still the tallest building in Australia, at 322.5 m. Its name is short for Queensland Number One. The design is said to draw on the Olympic torch, and its spire is lit at night. Near the top, an observation deck looks over the beaches of Surfers Paradise and the green hinterland. It was named one of Queensland's icons during the state's 150th birthday celebrations.

name: Speyer Cathedral
clues: The largest Romanesque church still standing, in red sandstone with four towers, where eight medieval emperors and kings lie in the crypt, beside the upper Rhine.
blurb: Emperor Conrad II began it in 1030 as a show of imperial power, and the east end and the vaults were built between 1090 and 1103. It is the largest Romanesque church still standing in the world, built of red sandstone with four towers and two domes. Eight emperors and German kings are buried in its crypt, along with several of their wives. French troops burned the town in 1689 and badly damaged it, and it was restored in later centuries. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1981.

name: Saint Catherine's Monastery
clues: The oldest home of monks still lived in, walled in granite at the foot of the mountain where Moses is said to have received the Ten Commandments, on a desert peninsula between two gulfs.
blurb: Byzantine Emperor Justinian I ordered it built between 548 and 565 at the foot of Mount Sinai, and it is the oldest Christian monastery that has been lived in without a break. Its thick granite walls enclose a bush said to be the burning bush seen by Moses. Centuries later, relics believed to be those of Catherine of Alexandria were brought here, and the monastery took her name. Its library holds one of the oldest and most important collections of early manuscripts in the world. Inside the walls there is even a small mosque.

name: Canterbury Cathedral
architect: William of Sens and William the Englishman
clues: Four knights murdered an archbishop at its altar in 1170, and for centuries pilgrims walked here telling each other tales on the way, not far from the white cliffs of the Channel.
blurb: Founded in 597, when Saint Augustine arrived to convert the Anglo-Saxons, it is the cathedral of the Archbishop of Canterbury, leader of the Church of England. It was rebuilt after the Norman Conquest and again, in Gothic style, after a fire in 1174, partly by William of Sens. In 1170 Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered inside by four knights, and his shrine made it one of the great pilgrimage sites of Europe. Chaucer's Canterbury Tales follows a group of pilgrims on their way here. It is part of a World Heritage Site.

name: Ryugyong Hotel
clues: A 330 m glass pyramid, begun in 1987 and still unopened, towers over the most secretive capital in East Asia: a hotel that has never had a single guest.
blurb: Construction of this 105-storey pyramid began in 1987, but work stopped in 1992 when the country's economy collapsed after the end of the Soviet Union. For 16 years it stood as a bare concrete shell without windows, nicknamed the 'hotel of doom'. Work resumed in 2008 and its glass skin was finished in 2011. It was meant to open in 2012, but it has still never welcomed a guest. At 330 m it dominates the skyline of Pyongyang, whose old name, Ryugyong, means 'capital of willows'.

name: El Escorial
architect: Juan Bautista de Toledo and Juan de Herrera
clues: The largest Renaissance building in the world, a stern granite palace, monastery and royal tomb all in one, in the hills north-west of an inland capital.
blurb: King Philip II built it between 1563 and 1584, about 45 km north-west of Madrid, as a monastery, palace and burial place for the Spanish kings all in one. Juan Bautista de Toledo began the design and Juan de Herrera finished it, in a plain, severe style later called Herrerian. It is the largest Renaissance building in the world. Its grid-like plan is said to recall the gridiron on which Saint Lawrence was martyred. Almost every Spanish king since Charles V lies in its royal pantheon, and its library is famous.

name: Museo del Prado
clues: Velázquez's Las Meninas and Goya's dark nightmares hang in this long Neoclassical gallery on a tree-lined boulevard of a high, dry inland capital.
blurb: Juan de Villanueva designed the building in 1785 as a natural history cabinet, but it opened in 1819 as a museum of paintings and sculpture, based on the Spanish royal collection. It holds the finest collection of Spanish art anywhere, with more works by Goya than by any other artist, along with Velázquez, El Greco, Bosch, Titian and Rubens. Highlights include Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya's Black Paintings and Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights. It stands on the Paseo del Prado, part of the city's 'Golden Triangle of Art'.

name: Umayyad Mosque
clues: Golden mosaics of riverside palaces line the courtyard of one of the oldest great mosques, said to hold the head of John the Baptist, in a city often called the oldest capital on Earth.
blurb: Caliph al-Walid I built it between 705 and 715 on a site that had held a Roman temple and then a church of John the Baptist. A shrine inside is said to hold the saint's head, honoured by Christians and Muslims alike. It is one of the oldest and largest mosques in the world, and its plan of a big courtyard and a long prayer hall shaped mosques across the Islamic world. Golden mosaics of trees, rivers and palaces cover parts of its walls. Medieval Muslim writers counted it among the wonders of the world.

name: Catherine Palace
clues: A sky-blue Rococo palace with a front over 300 m long and a room once lined entirely in amber, in the tsars' summer village south of a Baltic city.
blurb: Named after Catherine I, the wife of Peter the Great, it was rebuilt in its present Rococo form by Bartolomeo Rastrelli for Empress Elizabeth and finished in 1756. Its sky-blue and white front, decorated with gilded figures, is more than 300 m long. It was the summer residence of the tsars, at Tsarskoye Selo, about 30 km south of Saint Petersburg. Its most famous room was the Amber Room, lined with amber panels, which German troops carried off in the Second World War and which has never been found. A reconstruction opened in 2003.

name: Imam Ali Shrine
clues: A golden dome and two golden minarets crown the tomb of the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, visited by millions of pilgrims a year, on the desert edge west of the Euphrates.
blurb: Shia and Sunni Muslims believe it holds the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. Shia Muslims regard Ali as their first Imam, and the shrine is one of their holiest sites, visited by millions of pilgrims each year. Shia tradition also holds that Adam and Noah are buried beside him. The shrine has been rebuilt several times over the centuries, and its dome and minarets are covered in gold. The city of Najaf grew up around it and is still a great centre of Shia learning.

name: Church of Saint Sava
clues: One of the largest Orthodox churches anywhere, its white marble dome took most of a century to finish, on the spot where a saint's relics were burned, in a Balkan capital where two rivers meet.
blurb: It stands where, according to tradition, the Ottomans burned the relics of Saint Sava, the first Serbian archbishop and the nation's patron saint, in 1594. Construction began in 1935 but was halted by the Second World War and decades of communist rule. The outside was only finished in 2004, and the huge mosaic interior in 2020. It is one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world, faced in white marble and granite, with a central dome inspired by Hagia Sophia. Its gilded cross can be seen from across the city.

name: Gur-e-Amir
clues: A ribbed turquoise dome covers the tomb of a Turco-Mongol conqueror whose descendants later built the Taj Mahal, in an oasis city on the old Silk Road of Central Asia.
blurb: Begun in 1403 for Timur's grandson Muhammad Sultan, who died young, it became the tomb of Timur himself, the Turco-Mongol conqueror, after his death in 1405. Its ribbed, melon-shaped turquoise dome and blue tilework made it a model for later tombs built by his descendants, the Mughals, including Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal. Timur lies under a slab of dark green jade. Legend said a curse would strike anyone who opened his tomb; Soviet scientists did so in June 1941, days before Germany invaded the Soviet Union.

name: Transamerica Pyramid
clues: A tall white four-sided spike, tapering to a hollow spire between two wings, rising from a foggy, hilly city on a Pacific bay. For decades it was the tallest tower west of Chicago.
blurb: Designed by William Pereira and completed in 1972, the 48-storey pyramid was the tallest building in San Francisco until 2017. Its tapering shape was meant to let more light reach the streets than a boxy tower would. Two 'wings' on its sides hold the lift shafts and stairs, and a hollow spire crowns the top. Many locals disliked it at first, but it became the symbol of the skyline. The insurer Transamerica has moved its headquarters elsewhere, yet it still uses the building as its logo.

name: Galleria Borghese
clues: A cardinal built this villa to show off his art, and visitors still enter in timed slots to watch Bernini's marble come alive, in a park on a hill of an ancient southern capital.
blurb: Cardinal Scipione Borghese, nephew of Pope Paul V, had the villa built in the early 17th century to show his collection, and Flaminio Ponzio developed it from the cardinal's own sketches. It stood at the edge of Rome, inside the large park that still bears the family name. Its rooms hold Bernini's marble sculptures, such as Apollo and Daphne, along with paintings by Caravaggio, Raphael and Titian. The Italian state bought the house and its collection in 1902. Visitors must book a time slot, and numbers are limited.

name: Selimiye Mosque
clues: An architect of about 80 called this his masterpiece: one vast dome on eight piers, ringed by four needle-thin minarets, in a Thracian city close to two European borders.
blurb: Sultan Selim II commissioned it, and the great architect Mimar Sinan built it between 1568 and 1575, when he was about 80. Sinan considered it his masterpiece. Its huge dome rests on eight piers, giving an open, unified prayer hall, and its four slender minarets are among the tallest ever built. It stands on a hill in Edirne, a former Ottoman capital, near the borders with Greece and Bulgaria. Together with its complex of schools and other buildings, it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2011.

name: Philadelphia Museum of Art
architect: Horace Trumbauer with Zantzinger, Borie & Medary
clues: A film boxer ran up the stone steps of this golden Greek-temple museum and punched the air at the top, in the East Coast city where a nation declared independence.
blurb: The museum grew out of the Centennial Exposition of 1876, and its main building opened in 1928 on Fairmount hill, at the end of the Benjamin Franklin Parkway. Designed by Horace Trumbauer with Zantzinger, Borie and Medary, it looks like a group of Greek temples in golden stone. It holds over 240,000 objects from Europe, America and Asia. Its front steps became famous in the 1976 film Rocky, when Sylvester Stallone's boxer runs up them and raises his arms at the top. A statue of Rocky now stands nearby.

name: Stockholm Palace
clues: Built on the ashes of a castle called Three Crowns, this huge Baroque block is still a working royal palace, on the island old town of a Baltic capital.
blurb: It stands on the site of Tre Kronor, the 'Three Crowns' castle, which burned down in 1697. Nicodemus Tessin the Younger designed the new Baroque palace in the manner of the palaces of Rome, and after long delays the royal family moved in in 1754. With more than 1,400 rooms, it is one of the largest palaces in Europe. It holds the offices of the King and the Royal Court and is used for state occasions. Parts are open to visitors, including the treasury with the regalia.
